1:
Henry opens on the sabbath just ended, a day of rest to the buried Lord and a silent one, spent by his disciples in tears, the temple services never more an abomination than when the priests presiding had their hands full of his blood; then he marks the turn, that this sabbath is over and the first day of the week is the first day of a new world. Pseudo-Jerome says it by the light, the dawn standing between night's darkness and day's brightness, so the chief light shines on the chief of days. Gloss explains the delay: they worked at the ointment until sunset on the Friday, could not finish, and could not come by night.

The hour is the first difficulty, since one account has the sun risen and another has it still dark. Augustine denies any discrepancy, taking the words to mean not that the sun stood over the earth but that his rising had begun to light the eastern sky, the remains of darkness lessening as the brightness grew. Ellicott would rather harmonise them by a morning haze, or the gloom that had covered the city the day before. Robertson keeps both notes of time as this evangelist's own, a walk begun in the dark and ending as the sun came up. Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic name for that first glimmer, the hind of the morning, with the saying of the rabbi who watched it spread over the valley of Arbel and said the redemption of Israel would come so, by degrees, increasing the further it went.

What the spices mean is agreed and pressed hard. Barnes objects to calling them sweet, since myrrh and the rest were bitter and the original says only spices, then turns the errand into evidence: women carrying embalming stuff expected no rising, and that strengthens the case that it happened. Clarke makes the same argument from their failure to remember what had been told them plainly. Robertson adds that the sabbath had to be over before anything could be bought, this being a fresh supply beyond what was prepared before the rest. Gill and Lightfoot note the rabbinic rule, that anointing is lawful for the living on that day and not the dead. Theophylact explains the purpose medically, spices absorbing the body's moisture and so holding off corruption. Gregory and Bede prefer the figure, the fragrance of good works and prayer carried to the tomb by those who seek him, and Bede reads the stone rolled away as the opening of sacraments long shut under the letter of a law written on stone.

Their question about the stone is read as a verdict on their expectations: Robertson says plainly that people debating how to get in have no hope of a resurrection. Calvin agrees they came without due consideration, having watched the stone put in place and not thought of it until they were on the road, but will not let the fault stand, since holy zeal blinded them and God does not charge it. Wesley notes how little they knew, nothing of the seal or the guard, so the stone was the only trouble they foresaw, and Ellicott catches them with the words still on their lips as they look up and find it moved. Bede credits the other account with naming who moved it, and keeps the remark that it was great by office rather than bulk. On the young man within, Theophylact holds the angel seen outside on the stone and the one sitting inside to be the same, though he reports the view that the accounts concern different women; Augustine offers either two angels heard separately, or an entering that means only passing an enclosure before the stone. Gregory takes the side he sat on for the point, the left standing for this present life and the right for the life without end.
4:
One short clause about the size of the stone divides the commentators three ways. Barnes says flatly that the words belong to the previous verse, giving the reason for the women's question, and Clarke agrees, citing a Greek manuscript, three copies of the old Latin, the Syriac and an early historian as punctuating it so, and pointing out what follows from it: they knew the stone was beyond their strength, and without access to the body the spices they carried were useless. Ellicott finds that reading less natural than another, taking the remark instead as the evangelist's own explanation of why he wrote that the stone had been rolled away rather than simply taken off. Robertson keeps it with what follows for a different reason again, as the writer accounting for how startling the sight was, a thing that size lying open before them. He fills in the approach as well, the women walking up the hill with downcast eyes and heavy hearts until the problem they had been discussing is answered in front of them, and he notes the vivid present tense here where the parallel account uses a plain past.

The tomb itself is described from what was known of such places. Gill cites the rule by which Jewish sepulchres were cut large enough for people to walk into, and Barnes says the same more briefly, comparing them to the vaults of his own day, which is what makes the women's entering intelligible. On who met them inside, Ellicott simply registers the difference, that where one account says an angel of the Lord this one describes the form as a young man. Robertson makes the divergence into an argument. A young man here, an angel in the first Gospel, two men in the third: variations of that kind, he says, show that the narratives are independent of one another and so strengthen rather than weaken the evidence for the fact itself. He still offers a reconstruction, the angel seated on the stone at first and afterwards within on the right, with the third account catching a later moment when the two were standing; and he notes the robe described here as a white one where the parallel has dazzling apparel.

In the angel's words Robertson hears precision. The verb used to quiet the women is the very word that described their amazement a line earlier. The title Nazarene appears only in this Gospel at this point, used to identify Jesus to them by the name they knew. The participle rendered the crucified one carries what was his shame and has become his glory, taken up as such by the apostle who gloried in nothing else. And the announcement itself is a simple past, a bare statement that the thing happened, where the apostle writing later uses a perfect to hold him in the risen state he has not left. Ellicott observes what is missing, the fuller summons found elsewhere to remember what their Lord had told them in Galilee. Clarke takes up the name of reproach and runs with it: the Jews had used Nazarene as an insult, but since he was crucified under it the angel keeps it and the apostles keep it, and so it has gone ever since with names flung in derision, Quaker and Puritan and Methodist among them, until the mockery becomes the ordinary title. His conclusion is practical, that a man need not be scrupulous about what he is called, so long as the name carries no evil in it.
7:
The naming of Peter apart from the rest is felt by everyone to be deliberate, and read in two incompatible ways. Clarke takes the separation at face value and presses it hard: Peter is not counted among the disciples here because by denying his Lord he had forfeited the discipleship and every right belonging to an apostle, and is named on his own precisely as a penitent who must be told and restored. Barnes forbids exactly that inference. The words mean his disciples and especially Peter, and nothing in them removes him from the number; what they show is that the Lord who might justly have cast him off after the denial loved him still, having loved him once and loved him to the end, and sent word of the rising as the proof of it. Wesley says only what amazing goodness this was in one so often denied. Gill gives the message a pastoral motive, that Peter might be neither afraid nor ashamed to come with the others, and adds the detail that no other evangelist records it, which he connects with the tradition that this Gospel was published under Peter's own eye, so that the man who had most to lose by the telling made sure nothing was left out that aggravated his crime or magnified the mercy shown him. Robertson turns the same tradition around: the clause survives only here because Peter remembered the message gratefully, and it was that day's later meeting with him that turned doubt into certainty among the apostles. Gill notes too that one version puts his name first of all.

The flight from the tomb is described in a run of imperfects that Robertson will not let pass. The trembling did not merely come on the women but held them and kept hold; the words used here are trembling and ecstasy where the parallel account has fear and great joy, so the feelings were plainly mixed; and the silence is explained by a fear that continued, the tense carrying the state rather than the moment. He adds that the excitement was too great for ordinary speech, and that in the other telling the same women run to bring the disciples word, hushed but swift. Ellicott renders the clause literally, that trembling and amazement seized them. Gill notices that the word for quickly is missing from several of the old versions.

At this verse Robertson halts to set out the state of the text, and his verdict is unambiguous. The two oldest and best Greek manuscripts stop here, three Armenian copies stop here, and a handful of witnesses carry a shorter close instead of the familiar one, while others give one ending, or another, or both together. He judges that the facts, complicated as they are, argue strongly against the genuineness of the verses that follow, observing that there is little in them not already told in the first Gospel. What he will not accept is that the book was meant to stop at a sentence saying the women were afraid; he thinks the writer was interrupted, or that a leaf or column was torn from the end of the roll, and that the various endings are so many attempts to repair the loss.
9:
Where the note of time belongs is disputed. Gill holds that it marks the rising, not the appearing, the other pointing having been adopted only to avoid a supposed clash with another account, which he denies exists. Theophylact proposes that other pointing, stopping after the rising and reading the day with what follows; Robertson thinks the first more probable while granting the second makes good sense. Clarke reports that everything from this verse to the end is absent from a famous Greek manuscript and anciently from many others, and preserves the alternative close found in a later Syriac margin, where the women report briefly to those with Peter and the Lord afterwards sends out through them, from east to west, the holy and incorruptible preaching of eternal salvation. Robertson presses the internal evidence the same way: the verb used here of the Risen Christ is used nowhere else of him, the preposition governing the casting out of the demons is otherwise always different, the pronoun for she stands absolutely only here, the phrase for those who had been with him occurs in no other Gospel, and the description of Mary belongs properly to an earlier introduction. All of it, he concludes, suggests a hand other than the evangelist's.

That Mary should be first is treated as fitting, not accidental. Henry says the honour went to the woman forgiven much and loving much, and draws the rule that those who cleave closest see him soonest and see most of him. Bede sets it against the beginning, a woman having brought man into sin, so that she who first tasted death should first see the rising and not carry a perpetual reproach, the channel of guilt becoming the channel of grace. Pseudo-Jerome puts her with the harlots and publicans who enter the kingdom before the synagogue, as the thief did before the apostles. On her seven devils Gregory takes the number for totality, as seven days stand for all time, so that they mean every vice; Theophylact offers the sharper alternative of seven spirits set against the seven virtues, a spirit without fear, without wisdom, without understanding, each opposed to a gift of the Spirit. Gregory adds a figure for the rising itself: as Samson left Gaza at midnight and carried off its gates, the Redeemer came out of hell before daylight and took the gates with him.

The disciples' refusal to believe is read three ways. Barnes makes it evidence, since men who disbelieved the report were plainly not expecting a resurrection, not easily deceived, and convinced by nothing short of the clearest proof. Gregory had said the same long before, that their slowness is less their weakness than our strength, the doubt having drawn out the many proofs by which we are steadied when we read them. Calvin allows no such credit. They were bound by a shameful indifference and failed to recall what they had heard again and again; had the women brought word of something never foretold there would have been reason to hesitate over an incredible thing, but to treat as a dream what the Son of God had so often promised was, he says, stupidity. He adds that all the women carried the message, one evangelist singling out Mary without contradicting the rest. Clarke notes that the mourners were not the eleven only but the wider company, weeping for their Master and for having abandoned him; Gill makes the same point about who was told. Augustine, looking ahead to the two on the road, identifies the farm house with the village named elsewhere and explains the other form by the holding of their eyes, something laid on them and left until the breaking of bread. Pseudo-Jerome reads that walking as the labour of the active life, where faith sees through a glass, against the vision in which it will see face to face.
12:
The appearance itself is passed over quickly and everyone says so. Gill supplies from the fuller account what these two lines compress, the stranger joining the two on the road, opening the Scriptures to them as they walked, sitting down to meat at the journey's end, being recognised at that moment and vanishing. Barnes fixes the destination and explains the phrase about another form as meaning simply that he looked unlike himself, enough that they did not know him at first. Robertson is careful to rule out one reading of it: this was no transfiguration such as the one described earlier in the book, and the other account puts the failure not in a changed body but in eyes that were held. He notes that the connecting phrase used here occurs nowhere else in this Gospel, and that the story told here in two lines is told in full elsewhere.

The difficulty is in the last clause, that the eleven did not believe the two either. Lightfoot states it without softening. The men returning from that walk found the company in Jerusalem already saying that the Lord was risen indeed and had appeared to Simon, and the grammar of that other account will not let the words be taken any other way, since the case of the participle refers them plainly to the eleven and those gathered with them. So the same evening has the eleven announcing the resurrection in one telling and refusing to believe it in another. Clarke thinks the criticism worth setting out at length and reproduces it whole.

Two other ways of holding the accounts together are offered. Robertson allows the clash to stand as it is and draws the same conclusion he has drawn before, that where two narratives diverge like this they are plainly not copied from one another; he then suggests that belief was not uniform in the room, and that an element which discredited every report of the rising persisted, as it did later on the mountain in Galilee where some still doubted even while worshipping. Wesley takes the gentler line, that the testimony of these two, added to what Peter had already said, moved them somewhat, so that what is denied is not any belief at all but a settled one. Gill and Barnes both read the word for the rest as meaning those who had stayed behind in the city. Robertson sums the sequence up in a sentence, that the men fared no better at their hands than the women had.
14:
Gloss marks this the closing appearance, and that phrase makes trouble. Augustine will not take the last time to mean the last of all, since the final meeting came forty days later, when a rebuke for not believing the witnesses would make no sense to men who had often seen him; he reads it as the last showing of that day, at nightfall, when the pair back from the country found the company talking of the rising and some still unconvinced. Calvin agrees the reproof fits the first evening, and disputes the meal: a laid table at that hour is improbable and will not square with the account in which he asks whether they have anything to eat, so the word should mean only that they were gathered. He rejects as forced the attempt to narrow the rebuke to Thomas. Gill puts the appearance late on that same first day, after the two had returned.

The rebuke is then turned into an argument by nearly everyone. Barnes presses it hardest: men this hard to convince had not conspired, had given all up as lost at the death, and expected nothing, so their resistance is the strongest proof the rising was real, since men who hoped for it would have seized on the least evidence. Clarke says the same in fewer words, so sceptical a company crediting nothing without the fullest evidence, so that their unbelief proves the Gospel. Henry adds a motive the others do not: part of what kept them from believing was pride, the thought that if he were risen he would surely have shown himself first to them. Pseudo-Jerome reads the rebuke as surgery, faith put in place of unbelief and a heart of flesh in place of the stony one. Gregory takes the eating as the point, since he ate and then ascended, the act declaring the truth of the flesh.

On the commission the question is which occasion it was. Gill places it forty days later and in Galilee, and Robertson thinks it another report of the charge given on the mountain there; Ellicott notes that much here is distinct enough to suggest a different occasion. What every creature means is worked over too. Gregory takes it of man alone, who shares something with each order, existence with stones, life with trees, feeling with animals, understanding with angels. Lightfoot shows the phrase to be ordinary rabbinic usage for mankind and particularly for the Gentiles, and Clarke follows him there. Barnes draws out how hard that was, a command it took a special revelation to make Peter obey, and states the rule: wherever there is man the Gospel is to be preached. Wesley presses the absence of any limit further: if any creature in any age has not heard, then either those who should have preached or those who should have heard, or both, have made void the counsel of God. Theophylact takes it of believing and unbelieving alike.

The clause about baptism divides them sharply. Theophylact holds believing is not enough, the baptized having a perfect salvation the catechumen has not reached; Bede presses the logic to infants, who cannot believe for themselves and so believe by others, as they drew from others the sin baptism remits. Robertson argues the opposite from the silence: the second half threatens only the unbeliever and says nothing of the unbaptized, so condemnation rests on disbelief alone, baptism being the picture of the new life and not the means of it; and so weighty a sacramental doctrine would need firmer ground than a disputed ending. Wesley states it flatly, that the unbeliever perishes whether baptized or not. Ellicott cautions that the word rendered damned means condemned, and need not carry the irreversible sense English has acquired. Cyril of Jerusalem piles up the promises to the believer, who is not judged but has passed from death into life.
17:
Who was promised these signs is the question, and four of the witnesses answer it the same way. Gill says not all believers and not always, but some, and for a time, the signs being needed to establish the Gospel, with preaching ministers chiefly in view. Barnes narrows it to the apostles and those of the first age who had like power, and adds a rule of interpretation: the promise is kept if the signs followed in the case of any who believed, and nobody need suppose they were meant to follow in the case of all, so that an objector must prove they never happened at all before he can call the promise unfulfilled. Clarke names the same company and corrects the verb, which means accompany rather than follow. Calvin explains why the promise was made at that moment, that the disciples might not think this power inseparable from the bodily presence now leaving them, and insists that it was never held by every one of them, the gifts having been distributed variously and the working of miracles falling to few.

Wesley breaks with all four. He takes the believing here to be the same believing named in the sentence before, since it was not one faith by which the apostle was saved and another by which he worked wonders, and he holds that in every believer still there is a latent power of the same kind, every effect of prayer being in truth miraculous, though in most it goes unexerted through the smallness of their faith and the unworthiness of the world around them. He adds the observation that miracles were once helps to faith and have now become an object of it, and he is willing to cite a cure within living memory in a German town as evidence.

The particular signs are then handled with care, and mostly by restriction. Ellicott notes that the promise of new tongues is the only place in any Gospel where the Pentecostal gift takes this definite form, and Robertson that the word new is doubtful in the best text. On the serpents, Gill and Clarke both report copies that add in their hands, and Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all point to the same single recorded instance, the viper shaken off at Melita; Ellicott recalls that authority over serpents and scorpions had been granted once before. Barnes hedges the promise about with a condition, that such things happen when they are needed to establish religion, and Clarke likewise, that the proof is given when it may serve the cause of truth. About the poison they are more cautious still. Clarke reads the clause as covering what is drunk by mistake or accident, and Wesley states the limit bluntly, that it is not to be by a man's own choice, since God never calls anyone to try such experiments. Ellicott can find no instance of it in the New Testament at all and can offer only the old tradition of the poisoned cup handed to the fourth evangelist.

Robertson declines the whole passage. He reports the judgement that these verses fall away sharply from the level of the farewell words in the first Gospel, and that handling vipers and swallowing poison carry the reader into the twilight of apocryphal storytelling; and since he takes the evidence against the genuineness of this ending to be nearly conclusive, he holds it unwise to build anything on them.
19:
Augustine weighs whether the opening words fix this as the last speech on earth. They seem to, but the text does not read after he had thus spoken, so the clause might cover all the discourses together; he settles for the stricter sense only because of arguments made earlier, and concludes the ascension followed these words together with those preserved in the other evangelist's second book. Robertson supplies what the account leaves out: nothing here tells when or where, and the third Gospel alone sets the scene on Olivet at the end of the forty days. Clarke assumes the same forty days of converse, and Wesley pauses on the title Lord as peculiarly fitting here. Calvin observes that the first evangelist says nothing of the ascension and this one nothing of its place or manner, and draws a reason from the pattern of the appearances: as the risen Lord did not show himself indiscriminately, so he did not let everyone witness his going, meaning this mystery to be known by the preaching of the gospel rather than seen with eyes.

Gregory sets it beside the older ascent. Elias was raised only into the air, nearer the earth than the ether, and carried to some hidden region to wait until he returns at the end to pay the debt of death; and he went up in a chariot, which shows a mere man needs help from outside himself, where the Redeemer used no chariot and no angels, being carried above all things by the power of one who made them. Pseudo-Jerome puts it as a symmetry: he who came down from heaven to free our weakness went up above the heavens.

What the seat at the right hand means is guarded on every side. Barnes warns that God has no hands and that Jesus sits in no direction, the phrase being human speech for the highest honour, as the seat beside a prince was reckoned. Calvin agrees it is a metaphor for the power next to God and that we must not imagine a place, and puts it more strongly, that the title amounts to God's deputy, standing for the person of God; and he insists the clause was added to tell us Christ was raised not to enjoy rest at a distance from us but to govern the world for the salvation of believers. Henry finds two postures in one, rest because the work was finished and rule because the kingdom was entered, and hears the heavenly hosts receive him in state. Cyril of Jerusalem gathers the testimonies to that session from the other evangelist and two apostles.

The closing verse is read as the start of the sequel. Bede observes that this Gospel, beginning later with the preaching of John, also runs further forward, to the years in which the apostles sowed the word through the world; Gill traces that movement from Galilee to the city, then to Pentecost, then out again under the persecution after Stephen. Theophylact takes the last clause for a rule, that words are made good by deeds, and turns it into a prayer that Christ would work with us until we are perfect. Barnes and Clarke both describe the working together as help of more than one kind, Barnes listing miracles, removed obstacles and success given the message, Clarke dividing it into inward illumination and an outward conveying of the word to the hearer. Clarke then adds a limit his fellow Methodist would not: miraculous powers are no longer requisite, the Gospel having been sufficiently confirmed, though the co-operation itself remains indispensable, since without it no man preaches successfully and no soul is saved. Robertson ends on the text again, noting that three words in this last sentence are found nowhere else in the Gospels but are common in the apostle's letters, and setting out the shorter ending some manuscripts carry instead.
